newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Major barks, Europe moves on.
newsitem.headline: Major barks, Europe moves on.

text.p: Joking about the Spice Girls pop group and their endorsement of his party, slipping away to a local bar for a few pints of Guinness, Prime Minister John Major was in buoyant mood at this weekend's European Union summit.
Major's EU colleagues were in a good mood too -- but for completely different reasons.
Major, shrugging off civil war over Europe in his party and a byelection which cost him his majority, clearly enjoyed the opportunity to give his fellow leaders a piece of his mind.
Tearing up his prepared script, he lectured French president Jacques Chirac, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and other leaders about how they should run their economy and jobs market.

They listened politely but without much enthusiasm, then turned to the matters which did get their attention -- a landmark pact on budget discipline in a European single currency and a blueprint for closer integration across the bloc.
Major was left, as Britain's Guardian newspaper said, "trailing defiantly in (the) wake", uttering apocalyptic prophecies of doom and delay.
"If this decision (on a single currency) goes wrong, the damage right across Europe will be terrible, let there be no doubt whatsoever about that," he told a radio interviewer.
Major clearly revelled in his momentary escape from the seething cauldron of domestic politics.
But others put his good humour down to the end-of-term lightheartedness of a premier set to be ousted by voters.
Labour leader Tony Blair arrived for pre-summit talks with socialist leaders, every inch the premier in waiting.

Major was scornful, but he admitted what other leaders have been too tactful to state openly, saying: "There is no doubt that some of the socialist countries would prefer to deal with a socialist government in the United Kingdom."
The fact is, Major's isolation is not just on policy.

Apart from Chirac, pleased at Major's support of France's insistence on political control of budget discipline, about the only leader with whom his relations are warm is Conservative Spanish prime minister Jose Maria Aznar.

Even among fellow conservatives, Major does not have much of a fan club. Belgian prime minister Jean-Luc Dehaene was angered when Major blocked his elevation to the presidency of the European Commission, arguing he was too much of a federalist.
Relations with Irish premier John Bruton are complicated by Northern Ireland. Kohl is irritated by Major's constant carping.

The bulk of the rest are socialists, far closer to Blair. Indeed Dutch prime minister Wim Kok, Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky and Portuguese prime minister Antonio Guterres sent video messages of support to Blair's last party conference.
But any hopes of a sudden wave of British enthusiasm for all things European under a Labour government are premature.
A May election will leave him little time to get his party and the country ready to sign up for reforms branded an attack on Britain's sovereignty by Conservative Eurosceptics.
But even with an early election, Blair is not enough of a European enthusiast -- either by conviction or by electoral calculation -- to sign up for everything put before him.
